n: Nephi now applies Isaiah 29 to the last days. He widens the prophecy beyond Jerusalem: Gentiles and Jews everywhere, including those in the Americas, will be “drunken” with wickedness before the Lord sets things right.

f.g: A metaphor: sin that dulls judgment the way alcohol does.

n: Judgments of nature—thunder, earthquake, storm, fire—will visit the wicked. Isaiah’s original words described Jerusalem’s siege; Nephi sees a larger fulfillment at the end of the world.

f.g: “Lord of armies”—God as commander of heaven’s forces.

n: Nations that attack Zion will be like a hungry man who dreams of a feast and wakes up still starving. Their schemes to destroy God’s people will come to nothing.

f.g: The holy mount of Jerusalem; in latter-day usage also the gathered, covenant people of God.

n: The wicked will be stunned and stagger as if drunk—not from wine, but from spiritual confusion they brought on themselves.
Because people closed their eyes and rejected the prophets, God let a “deep sleep” settle over them, and their seers were taken away. Spiritual blindness follows refusing light.

f.g: Prophets who see spiritual realities, past or future; compare Mosiah 8:15-17.

n: Into that sleepy world God will bring “the words of a book” written by people now dead. Latter-day Saints understand this as the Book of Mormon, written by ancient prophets.

f.g: Those who have died—here the Nephite prophets whose record speaks from the dust.

n: Part of the book will be sealed, containing a revelation of the whole history of the world from beginning to end.

f.w: from the beginning of the world to the ending thereof

n: The sealed portion will be withheld while the world is wicked. God reveals greater truths only when people are ready to receive them.

f.w: the book shall be kept from them

n: The book will be given to one man, who will pass some of its words to another. This matches Joseph Smith giving a copy of characters to Martin Harris.

f.w: he shall deliver these words unto another

n: The man will not hand over the book or its sealed portion. It stays sealed by God’s power until the Lord’s own timing.

f.w: own due time of the Lord

n: A day will come when the sealed words are read openly, “upon the house tops,” and everything that has ever happened among humanity will be made known.

The book will be hidden from the public, but three witnesses besides the translator will see it by God’s power and testify of it. This was fulfilled in Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris.
A few others will also see it as God allows, to add their testimony. The Eight Witnesses handled the plates and wrote their own statement.

f.g: Fulfilled in part by the Eight Witnesses, whose testimony appears in the front of the Book of Mormon.

f.w: as if it were from the dead

n: God establishes truth through multiple witnesses, and warns those who reject his word. The principle of witnesses runs throughout scripture.

f.w: in the mouth of as many witnesses

n: The unsealed words will be shown to a learned man who asks for the book itself. Latter-day Saints connect this with Martin Harris showing the characters to scholar Charles Anthon in 1828.
Nephi exposes the learned man’s motive: worldly reputation and profit, not God’s glory.

f.g: To make money or advantage for oneself.

n: The man explains that the book cannot be brought because it is sealed.
The learned man answers, “I cannot read it”—Anthon’s reported reply to Martin Harris was nearly the same.
So God gives the book to a man who is not learned—Joseph Smith, a young farmer with little schooling—who humbly admits his lack of learning.
God reassures him: the scholars have rejected the work, but God can do it himself. The unlearned man will read words God gives him—translation by divine gift, not scholarship.

f.w: I am able to do mine own work

n: The translator must leave the sealed portion alone. God will bring it out when he chooses, proving he can do his own work.

f.w: Touch not the things which are sealed

n: After translating and showing the plates to the witnesses, the man must return the book into God’s keeping. Joseph Smith gave the plates back to the angel Moroni.
God declares he is a God of miracles, unchanging across time, and that he works among people according to their faith.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever

n: Nephi introduces another message the Lord will give to the man who reads the book.
People honor God with their words but their hearts are far away, and their reverence comes from human traditions. Jesus quoted this verse, and the Lord echoed it to Joseph Smith in the First Vision.

f.w: draw near unto me with their mouth

n: Because of this, God will do “a marvelous work and a wonder”—the restoration of the gospel—that will outshine the wisdom of the worldly wise.
Those who plot in secret think no one sees them. God compares them to clay telling the potter he doesn’t exist. The creation cannot outsmart its Creator.

f.g: Twisting matters, perverting what is right.

n: Soon the land itself will be transformed: Lebanon’s forest becomes a fruitful field. Many read this as a picture of the gathering and renewal of Israel in the last days.

f.w: Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field

n: Those who were spiritually deaf and blind will hear and see through the book. The Book of Mormon brings light out of obscurity.

f.w: out of obscurity and out of darkness

n: The humble and the poor will find joy in the Lord. The gospel is good news especially for the meek.

f.g: A favorite title of Isaiah for God; Nephites understood it as Christ (2 Nephi 25:29).

n: The tyrant and the mocker will be brought down, and those who look for chances to do evil will be removed.
Also judged: those who trap people over a single word, ensnare the one who rebukes evil at the city gate, and deny justice to the righteous over trivial excuses.

f.g: The city gate was where court was held; this is the honest judge or witness.
For nothing; on a flimsy pretext.

n: The Lord who redeemed Abraham promises that Jacob—Israel personified—will no longer be ashamed or pale with fear.

f.g: Turn pale, as from shame or fear.

n: When Israel sees its descendants gathered and faithful, they will honor God’s holy name together.
Those who were confused will understand, and complainers will learn true doctrine—a hopeful ending showing what the book will accomplish.
